title: Interior and Wardrobe
premise: Ulyana Fairweather, a translator who has spent thirty years sanding down her mother's dying language into polite English, is hired by Halvard Ness, the last fluent speaker of Vessic, to become his final student before his house—and its archive of recordings—is sold. As lessons deepen into something like love, Ulyana discovers her own grandmother's voice on his tapes, revealing that her family's silence was a deliberate severance, not an accident. When the sale closes early and Halvard's health collapses, she must return to the coastal village where her story went wrong, confront the aunt who chose duty over belonging, and decide whether a language can survive in one speaker, one student. The novel ends with Ulyana teaching her niece a single Vessic word at Halvard's grave—small, imperfect, but no longer invisible.
about_author: A. M. Montrose is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages and claims fluency in neither. They live near the sea and write about the words people bury in order to belong.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. At a London literary gala, she translates flawlessly for a celebrated novelist while deflecting every personal question with her practiced smile. A stranger asks where she's 'really' from; she gives the answer that ends conversations. Beat: establish her armor of professional invisibility and the loneliness beneath it.

chapters.title: A Letter in a Dying Alphabet
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A handwritten letter arrives in Vessic script—the first she's seen since childhood—from one Halvard Ness, requesting a meeting. She translates it three times, each version more honest. Beat: the past knocking; she almost files it under work.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. In a cluttered coastal cottage, ninety-one-year-old Halvard explains: he is the last fluent speaker of Vessic, and he wants one final student—not a linguist, someone with the language already buried in them. He plays a tape; Ulyana hears her grandmother's voice. Beat: shock cracking the armor.

chapters.title: Terms of Study
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She negotiates like a contract translator—hours, fees, boundaries—but Halvard insists lessons happen in his kitchen, over food, in the old way. She agrees to six weeks, telling herself it's research. Beat: cautious commitment disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Halvard's POV. He watches Ulyana reach for Vessic words and flinch when they arrive whole. He catalogs what she's lost: kinship terms, lullabies, the word for the space between tide and shore. Beat: tenderness mixed with diagnostic grief for a language losing its speakers.

chapters.title: What the Tapes Keep
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Cataloging Halvard's archive, she finds recordings from 1974 labeled with her grandmother's maiden name. She listens to one minute and stops. Beat: dread; the discovery that her family knew Halvard intimately.

chapters.title: Six Weeks, Then Home
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Lessons settle into rhythm: grammar at dawn, stories at dusk. Halvard teases her perfectionism; she catches herself laughing. Her partner Marcus calls with news that her flat sale is progressing—a life being packed up elsewhere. Beat: warmth arriving against her will.

chapters.title: The Word for Staying
chapters.summary: Halvard's POV. He teaches the Vessic verb that means both 'to remain' and 'to be kept,' and watches Ulyana write it down twice. He remembers another student, fifty years ago, who left. Beat: the theme of staying versus leaving made explicit through language.

chapters.title: Aunt Vera's Telephone Voice
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Her aunt Vera calls from the village: the house sale is moving faster than expected, and Halvard's name appears in the estate papers. Vera's voice goes flat when Ulyana mentions the lessons. Beat: the family's sealed history pressing against its lid.

chapters.title: Tape 41
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Alone at night, she plays Tape 41: her grandmother, young and laughing, arguing with Halvard about a word for grief. Between the lines, an older woman's voice—her great-grandmother—speaks of sending the children away so they'd 'sound like everyone.' Beat: the wound located; duty severed belonging deliberately.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Kitchen
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Ulyana accuses Halvard of knowing all along why she was chosen. He admits it: her grandmother asked him, before she died, to find whoever inherited her silence. Ulyana walks out into the rain. Beat: midpoint rupture; trust broken by truth.

chapters.title: Marcus, Practical and Kind
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Marcus visits, sees the tapes spread everywhere, and gently suggests she finish the job, sell everything, move on—as they've always done. She realizes their whole relationship runs on her talent for leaving. Beat: love measured against the pattern of escape.

chapters.title: The House Sale Accelerates
chapters.summary: Halvard's POV. The buyer's solicitor pushes completion forward; Halvard's heart stumbles on the stairs and he hides it. He begins recording farewell messages in Vessic, one per day, addressed to a student who isn't speaking to him. Beat: ticking clock tightened; mortality enters.

chapters.title: Return to the Village Where It Went Wrong
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She takes the coast road back to the village she left at nine years old, after the incident she's never named even to herself: the day she refused to speak Vessic at her grandfather's funeral and meant it. Beat: homecoming as excavation.

chapters.title: Vera's Version
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Aunt Vera, over cold tea, tells her side: the family was punished after the war years for the old tongue; sending the children away was protection dressed as progress. Vera has regretted it for sixty years and never learned how to say so. Beat: antagonist revealed as fellow casualty of duty.

chapters.title: The Funeral Tape
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. In Halvard's archive she finds the recording of her grandfather's funeral—her own nine-year-old voice refusing the eulogy. Hearing it as an adult, she hears not betrayal but terror. Beat: climax of memory; self-forgiveness becomes possible.

chapters.title: Hospital Light
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Halvard has collapsed; she reaches his hospital room as the sale completes downstairs in the solicitor's office. He can barely speak English; she must use Vessic to understand him. Beat: crisis forcing the language—and the love—into the open.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Halvard asks her, in Vessic, to stop studying and start living the language—to take the remaining tapes not as archive but as inheritance. Ulyana chooses him, and it, over the tidy life waiting in London. Beat: emotional climax; the choice made aloud in a dying tongue.

chapters.title: What the Buyer Bought
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The new owner of Halvard's house turns out to be a heritage developer planning a 'language museum.' Ulyana negotiates fiercely—not for money but for the kitchen table, the tape shelf, the right of return. Beat: external stakes resolved through earned authority.

chapters.title: The Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Halvard's POV. Back home under hospice care, Halvard gives his final lesson: no grammar, only the story of the word for the space between tide and shore, which he finally finishes. He dies at dusk with Ulyana reciting beside him. Beat: elegiac peak; transmission completed.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Language
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. After the funeral, she catalogues what remains: 412 hours of tape, one notebook, two speakers' worth of memory, herself. She ends things gently with Marcus and declines the prestigious translation post. Beat: quiet reckoning; the old life dismantled without drama.

chapters.title: One Word, Given Away
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A year later, she teaches her young niece the Vessic word for the space between tide and shore, on the beach below Halvard's sold-but-remembered house. The girl mispronounces it beautifully. Beat: resolution—belonging rebuilt not as preservation but as gift; the language lives, changed, in one more mouth.
